title: Solo dev, building an idle RPG that lives in phone widgets with Gemini for art and Claude Code for the code. Here's my pipeline and where it breaks
author: sozkan41
selftext:
Hi all. I'm a solo developer from Turkey and for the past few weeks I've been building **Widget Fangs**, a vampire vs werewolf idle RPG that mostly lives on your phone's home screen. You hunt for 15–20 minutes when you're bored, and the rest of the time your character works night shifts and expeditions on its own while the widget shows what happened. Vampires get stronger in your real local night, werewolves on the real full moon.

I can write apps, but I can't draw. So the whole project is basically an experiment in how far one person can get with generative AI on both sides: art and code. I wanted to share the workflow, because some parts worked much better than I expected and some parts are honestly still a mess.

**Art: Gemini + a small pipeline**

All character art comes from Gemini. Generating images one by one in the chat got old fast, so I wrote a small userscript that reads a JSON list of jobs (name, folder, prompt, aspect ratio) and runs them in order, saving each result with a predictable filename. A Python script then picks them up, removes the background with rembg (isnet model + alpha matting), trims it and writes a webp straight into the game's asset folders. The image above is one character going through that: raw output, cut-out, and sitting on top of a real widget in the game.

That gave me a few hundred images so far: 8 classes in male and female versions, enemies, NPCs, loot, crates, widget art. The daily generation limit is the real bottleneck; a 60-image batch usually doesn't fit in a single day.

What didn't work: consistency. Batches made on different days drift in style, faces and proportions. I also got the classic anatomy bugs (a character with three hands, a sitting pose with tangled legs), so every character prompt now has an explicit "exactly two arms, two hands" rule, and I review everything before it goes in. Another lesson: never let the model render text or UI. All the widget UI is real, drawn by the app, and the AI art is composited around it.

**Code: Claude Code as a small "team"**

The app is Flutter with native widgets (Jetpack Glance on Android, WidgetKit and Live Activities on iOS), and the backend is Firebase with Cloud Functions. The economy is fully server-authoritative: the client only sends requests, the server decides loot, RNG and time, so nobody can edit their gold on the device.

I run Claude Code as a main agent that never writes code itself. It splits each feature into small packages (one goal, max \~5 files), hands them to specialised sub-agents (mobile, Android, server, site, tests, translation, balance, iOS on a separate Mac session) and then reviews the result. A code knowledge graph keeps the agents from re-reading the whole repo every time. Balance numbers live in one config file and get checked with a Python economy simulator before any change. This structure is what made a project of this size possible for one person; without it the agents kept losing context and "fixing" things nobody asked for.

For marketing I use Flow / Veo image-to-video on the same game art (the widget clip in my posts is the real widget with an animated character on top).

**Where I'd love your input**

1. How do you keep a consistent style across hundreds of images and multiple days? Reference sheets, fixed seeds, a fine-tuned model? I'm planning to regenerate everything in one consistent pass once the systems settle, and I'd rather do it right once.
2. Anyone else running multi-agent setups for game code? How do you stop agents from drifting outside their task?

The game is in a free closed alpha on iOS and Android (no purchases enabled). If you want to see how it all holds together on a real phone: [https://widgetfangs.com](https://widgetfangs.com). Shake the device on any screen to send a bug report. Happy to answer questions about any part of the pipeline.
